stories.headline: Update: Container Ship Sinks in Strait of Hormuz After Being Hit by Projectile
stories.summary:
A Singapore-flagged container ship, the GFS Pride, sank after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Singaporean maritime authorities said. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported, though the attack caused damage and a fire. A second Singapore-flagged vessel, the GFS Giselle, was hit on Wednesday and sustained hull damage but reached a safe anchorage with all 22 crew.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the strait. They released photos showing black smoke rising from a container vessel and dozens of containers floating in the water. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said two other container ships reported being struck by unknown projectiles on Tuesday and continued their passages with minor damage. Separately, maritime risk group Vanguard said the bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after being hit on 23 September, an attack that killed one seafarer.

Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack since the US-Israel war with Iran began in February. The International Maritime Organization counts at least 24 seafarers killed in 106 confirmed incidents. A fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass through the strait, which was effectively closed early in the war. A preliminary US-Iran agreement in June to end the war and reopen the strait collapsed within weeks, and Iran has since targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route.

stories.headline: US Inflation Rises to 3.7% in September, Above Forecasts, on Gasoline Surge
stories.summary:
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August and above forecasts, according to official figures. It was the final inflation report before next month's midterm elections, which are being fought largely over cost-of-living pressures. The Bureau of Labor Statistics said gasoline was the main driver.

Car fuel prices jumped 34.2% over twelve months and 9.1% in September alone, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase. Energy inflation overall was 20.4% over the year, with fuel oil up 74.2%. Crude oil is currently above $100 a barrel, compared with just over $70 before the US-Israel war with Iran constricted supplies through the Middle East.

Outside energy, price pressures remain more contained. Food inflation was flat in September and 2.5% over the year, while core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%. Experts said the Federal Reserve will watch closely for signs that higher energy costs spread to other areas of the economy. Shortly after the data release, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027.

stories.headline: Supreme Court to Weigh Whether Cooking for Terrorists Bars Asylum
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear the Trump administration's bid to deny asylum to Izuchukwu Ozurumba, a Nigerian man whom officials say provided material support to terrorists by cooking for them. The case centers on an immigration provision barring entry to people who have "engaged in terrorist activity," a term that includes material support.

Ozurumba says he took a camp cook job in 2022 before learning the camp was run by a separatist group called the Unknown Gunmen. He says he worked there about six months, half of it unpaid, before escaping, and that members later threatened to kill him. An immigration judge rejected his asylum claim, finding that cooking three meals a day was material support. He was deported in April 2025, but the 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in his favor five months later, saying cooking did not qualify.

His lawyer, Aimee Mayer-Salins of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said the administration's broad reading would make it very hard for people fleeing persecution to seek safety in the US, since even the most insignificant support could trigger a bar. The administration has cracked down on asylum claims as part of its broader immigration policy. The justices will hear arguments and rule by the end of the term in June, and in coming weeks will also decide whether to take up the administration's appeal to maintain a broad block on asylum claims at the US-Mexico border.

stories.headline: Netflix to Lay Off 1,000 Staff in Steepest Cuts Since 2022
stories.summary:
Netflix said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally, about 6% of its workforce, in its largest round of layoffs since 2022. The cuts will mainly affect human resources, legal, product and technology teams. Managers will tell affected employees "soon."

In an email to staff, co-chief executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said the company would continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas and that it remains on track to meet its financial forecasts. Last month Sarandos said Netflix was "not growing as fast as I want us to." The company reports quarterly results on 20 October.

The streaming industry is consolidating after Paramount's $110 billion merger with Warner Bros., a deal for which Netflix had also bid before being outbid. Free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to draw viewers. Analyst Ross Benes of eMarketer said Netflix has not found another major revenue line and is nearing a ceiling on its subscription business. The last major layoff round, in 2022, cut about 450 jobs after the company lost subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

stories.headline: Judge extends White House press access for MS Now, CNN and Politico indefinitely
stories.summary:
A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction late Tuesday extending White House press access for three news outlets targeted by President Donald Trump: MS Now, CNN and Politico. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, found the outlets would likely succeed on the merits of their First Amendment lawsuit against the administration.

Kelly determined that the journalists' press passes were likely revoked without due process. The injunction keeps the access in place while the case proceeds, rather than for a fixed period.

The ruling is an early legal test of how far the executive branch can go in controlling which news organizations may cover the president from inside the White House. Press freedom advocates and the affected outlets have argued that revoking credentials without a fair process amounts to punishing coverage the administration dislikes. The administration has previously maintained that it has broad discretion over access to White House facilities and over who is credentialed.

The case is expected to continue in district court on the underlying claims, and the administration could appeal the preliminary injunction. The fact that the ruling came from a Trump-appointed judge is likely to figure prominently in the debate over the decision, with critics of the administration citing it as evidence of the strength of the First Amendment claims and the administration's defenders expected to stress the limits of judicial authority over press-office decisions.

stories.headline: Treasury fines Bank of America $1.2 billion over sanctions and anti-money laundering violations
stories.summary:
The Treasury Department announced Tuesday afternoon, after markets closed, that it is imposing more than $1.21 billion in penalties on Bank of America for violations of sanctions and anti-money laundering laws. Treasury said the violations included facilitating payments that may have involved Chinese money laundering networks and criminals operating on the southern border.

The penalty is the third-largest ever imposed by the Treasury. Officials described the action as part of the administration's broader effort to pursue banks that fail to meet their sanctions and anti-money laundering obligations.

The size of the fine makes it a significant enforcement signal to the financial industry, where compliance programs are closely watched for how regulators weigh failures to detect illicit flows. The announcement's timing after the close of trading means market reaction to the penalty will emerge in Wednesday's session. Details on any remedial requirements or the bank's response were not included in the available reporting.

stories.headline: Ukraine says Starlink speed limits on military terminals hamper defense against Russian drones
stories.summary:
Ukrainian officials say speed limits were imposed without warning on military-grade Starlink terminals, disrupting missions and forcing the cancellation of some drone operations. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology, said the restrictions apply to Starshield, SpaceX's military service, and limit terminals moving faster than 100 mph. Starshield satellites are owned and controlled by the U.S. Department of War.

Beskrestnov warned the limits could undermine air defenses, particularly interceptor units used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. "Our defense forces received no warning," he wrote. He also said the move was "no coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," pointing to friction between Zelensky and President Donald Trump, a close ally of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, over an energy ceasefire. Ukraine told SpaceX the restriction was not previously in place and has created significant operational challenges.

Neither SpaceX nor Musk has publicly confirmed the restrictions, and SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Musk whether he was "playing politics with your products again" and warned that European customers were watching. The dispute comes as Russia and Ukraine continue trading attacks despite Trump's announced energy ceasefire, with Kyiv saying it received no advance warnings from allies for a second day.

stories.headline: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on spying charges
stories.summary:
Russian authorities have arrested Yuki Imai, a journalist with Japan's Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, on suspicion of espionage. He was detained in the far-eastern Sakhalin region a day before he was due to leave Russia, then flown to Moscow, where a court ordered pre-trial detention until 12 December, according to Russian news agencies.

The FSB alleges Imai acted on instructions from Japan's national intelligence service to gather information on Russian defense capabilities and on people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands. The agency published footage showing masked men storming a hotel room. Those convicted of espionage in Russia can face up to 20 years in prison. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Tokyo's attempts to use correspondents to gather information were regrettable and that the incident was "not an isolated one."

Japan says it learned of the arrest only upon the announcement and has not been able to contact Imai. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo is seeking details, and the newspaper said ensuring the reporter's safety is its top priority. The arrest comes amid worsening relations after President Vladimir Putin's August visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sharply criticized as wounding the feelings of the Japanese people.

stories.headline: Turkish Police Raid Opposition Halk TV, Halting Live Broadcasts
stories.summary:
Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of Halk TV on Wednesday, halting the pro-opposition channel's live broadcasts. Employees said they were unable to enter the building and that a new manager had been appointed to run the channel. Turkish media reported that financial crimes police searched the premises and that 11 people were taken into custody.

Prosecutors issued arrest warrants for 17 people as part of an investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroglu, who is accused of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering. Mahiroglu, who was reportedly abroad during the raid, said seven members of his family were among those detained. "Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons."

The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, noting it came hours before Ekrem Imamoglu, widely seen as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's biggest rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court. He has been in prison for more than a year. Ozgur Ozel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly" and said that storming a channel and appointing a trustee "is something only dictators do." Ozel founded the party after a court removed him as leader of the Republican People's Party (CHP).

Turkey ranks 163rd of 180 countries in the 2026 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, which says 90 percent of national media outlets are under government control. The government has not been quoted in the available reporting, and the allegations against Mahiroglu are for the courts to decide.

stories.headline: Germany Puts Ukrainian on Trial Over Nord Stream Pipeline Sabotage
stories.summary:
A Ukrainian man identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K went on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday, accused of blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea in September 2022. He is the first suspect to stand trial over the blasts, which destroyed three of the four pipelines off the Danish island of Bornholm. He was extradited to Germany last year and denies the charges, as does a second suspect fighting extradition from Croatia.

Prosecutors allege he plotted with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and cut off Russia's gas revenue, and that the saboteurs acted "by order of Ukrainian state agencies." Investigators focused on divers who rented a yacht, the Andromeda, from the port of Rostock, and said traces of subsea explosives were found on the boat. Prosecutors are treating the attack as a war crime, an attack by military means on civilian objects. Germany's federal court of justice ruled in January 2025 that the case fell within German jurisdiction because it involved undermining the country's internal security.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has long maintained Ukraine had nothing to do with the blasts. Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, argued the attack took place during wartime and that Nord Stream 2 was a tool Russia used to prepare for its invasion. Russian President Vladimir Putin had blamed the United States and Britain, which both denied involvement.

The trial is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies, and has exposed differing views in Berlin and Kyiv on the case.

stories.headline: Saudi Engineer Charged With Planting Recording Device in OpenAI Office
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors have charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who worked as an engineer at OpenAI, with secretly planting a recording device in the company's San Francisco office. He is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He appeared in court on Tuesday, and it is unclear whether he has legal representation. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

According to the complaint, the encrypted device was wrapped in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI employees found it on September 30, two days after prosecutors say it was installed. The company said it used its own AI models to analyze the device and identify the employee who planted it. FBI Director Kash Patel said the alleged goal was to capture sensitive information about the company's AI products.

Prosecutors say Alfozan, employed since July 2025, used a chatbot to research how to build, customize, encrypt and remotely access an audio recorder. CCTV footage allegedly shows him returning to inspect the device on October 5, and the same day a bag he left unattended was found to contain his wallet, ID and a similar recording device.

OpenAI said it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were accessed, and that the employee has been fired. The case adds to concerns about insider threats and espionage at leading AI companies.

stories.headline: Update: Russian Strikes Leave 600,000 Without Power in Ukraine Despite Trump's 'Energy Ceasefire'
stories.summary:
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine are without electricity after overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. He said critical energy infrastructure was hit in Kyiv, its surrounding region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv. In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, according to the state emergency service.

Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones overnight, with four missiles and 115 drones shot down. Russia's defence ministry said its strikes targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military, and claimed to have downed 902 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions including Moscow and Crimea.

The attacks came despite President Donald Trump's Sunday announcement of an "energy ceasefire" that he said both sides had accepted. Zelensky has repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russian refineries and energy sites if Moscow does the same. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the respite a truce would bring, arguing Europe would use it to arm Kyiv further.

The new strikes raise questions about whether the announced ceasefire has any practical effect, and about Washington's leverage over Moscow. Russia controls roughly 20 percent of Ukrainian territory following its 2022 full-scale invasion.
